Diagnosed Jekyll configuration issues and architected documentation solution.

Jekyll's documentation confirms that only files with YAML front matter get processed as special files, meaning the chapter files without front matter will be copied directly into the built site unchanged. —ated website when published via GitHub Pages. The root URL would likely return a 404, and individual chapter files would serve as raw markdown text without any styling from the theme, completely undermining the purpose of the Jekyll configuration.

The fix is straightforward: add YAML front matter with layout: default and a title to every markdown file, and create an index.md file (or add front matter to README.md with a permalink directive) so the site has a proper homepage. This ensures Jekyll processes each file through the theme and renders them as styled HTML pages instead of serving raw markdown.

There's an important nuance here: README.md should stay without front matter so it displays correctly when viewed directly on GitHub.com's repo page—adding front matter would cause the literal --- delimiters to show up as visible text in the repo view, since GitHub.com's own README renderer doesn't strip Jekyll syntax. The cleanest solution is to keep README.md as-is and create a separate index.md file with front matter that mirrors the README content, giving the Pages site a proper homepage while preserving the repo's README display.

This approach matches established Jekyll/GitHub Pages best practices, and implementing it means adding front matter to the 9 chapter files plus the epilogue, then creating that new index.md. I've found a real issue: the navigation links embedded in the chapter content itself—like the "← Chapter 1" and "Proceed to Chapter 3 →" links at the bottom of each chapter, plus the directory list in the index—aren't being automatically converted from .md to .html by Jekyll the way the main navigation is, so they're still pointing to the literal markdown files in the rendered output.

This means clicking those in-story navigation links would actually try to load /chapter-2.md directly from the server, which GitHub Pages wouldn't render as HTML—it would either serve it as plain text or trigger a download depending on MIME type configuration. This is a separate bug from the front-matter issue, and it requires either manually rewriting all those internal links to use no-extension permalinks or using a Jekyll plugin to handle the conversion automatically.

Summary

This site would not have worked at all as originally uploaded — no anecdotal concern, actually built it with real Jekyll 4.3.2 and confirmed:

  1. No index.html in the built output at all. Visiting the site's root URL would 404. Root cause: none of the files (including README.md) had YAML front matter, and Jekyll only processes/renders files that have it — confirmed both via Jekyll's own official docs and by directly inspecting the built _site/ output.

  2. Every chapter would serve as raw, unrendered markdown text, not styled HTML — _site/chapter-1.md contained the literal ## CHAPTER 1: source, no theme, no HTML conversion. Confirmed by building the actual site and reading the actual output file.

  3. A second, independent bug: even after adding front matter, the in-story navigation links ([Proceed to Chapter 2 →](chapter-2.md)) rendered as literal href="chapter-2.md" — pointing at a raw file, not the rendered page. Fixed with jekyll-relative-links, which I confirmed is on GitHub Pages' actual whitelisted-plugin list (checked directly against GitHub's own pages-gem source), so this fix will genuinely take effect on the real published site, not just locally.

What I did:

  • Added front matter to all 9 chapter/epilogue files
  • Created a separate index.md for the actual homepage, deliberately leaving README.md untouched — adding front matter to README.md itself would make the literal ---\nlayout: ...\n--- block show up as visible text when the repo is browsed normally on GitHub.com, which is a known, documented gotcha (confirmed via a real-world example repo using this exact separation pattern)
  • Fixed the two README.md-specific links (in chapter-1 and the epilogue) to point at index.md instead
  • Enabled jekyll-relative-links in _config.yml

Verified, not assumed: rebuilt the complete site after every change and grepped every single generated HTML page for any remaining broken .md links — zero found. _config.yml is restored to the actually-intended jekyll-theme-midnight (I only swapped to minima temporarily for local testing, since jekyll-theme-midnight isn't installable in this particular sandbox — but it's fully supported on GitHub Pages' real infrastructure).

LICENSE is genuine, verbatim CC0 1.0 text, and all chapter titles/ordering match the README's table of contents exactly — no changes needed there.

Full read-through — honest assessment

The story itself is genuinely well-crafted. The technical/narrative parallel is consistent and clever throughout — real commands (kill -9, sysrq triggers, Cisco ACLs, a literal fork bomb) doing double duty as both plausible sysadmin actions and escalating weapons against a reality-editing "compiler." The prose voice stays controlled and specific rather than drifting into vague horror-adjacent hand-waving, and the ending lands on the right note thematically — "PARTIAL" integrity, permanent artifacts, no clean save — which pays off the "uninstalled, not haunted" framing from Chapter 1.

Three things worth fixing, found by actually reading rather than just checking structure:

  1. Typo, Chapter 3: "The screen frozen. The cursor stayed solid." — should be "The screen froze." (participle used where the simple past tense is needed).

  2. A real continuity gap between Chapters 6 and 7. Chapter 6 ends with unambiguous, conclusive victory language: "Process BIOLOGICAL_COMPILER_v0x7F terminated," "He was no longer the gateway." Chapter 7 then opens with the same crisis fully active again — the cold needle, the 512ms polling cadence, a COGNITIVE_BRIDGE_ABHRANKAN process mid-overflow — with zero acknowledgment that this is a distinct, deeper threat rather than the same one somehow un-resolved. It's possible this is intentional (the compiler process dies in Ch6, but the underlying bridge infrastructure it exploited is a separate, still-live problem revealed in Ch7) — but as written, there's no transitional sentence signaling that distinction, so it reads as a discontinuity rather than an escalation. Worth either adding a bridging line at the top of Ch7 (something establishing "the compiler was dead, but the bridge it had ridden in on was still open") or reconsidering the chapter order/framing.

  3. Epilogue paragraph-merge bug, confirmed above — just needs a blank line added between the two sentences-blocks.

GitHub repo name, description, topics/tags, commit message, version tag, and release notes?

Repo name: foxpunch

Description:

Stateless UDP relay for NAT hole-punching — proof of concept for a Tailscale/WireGuard-style peer-to-peer tunnel foundation.

License: MIT — consistent with the rest of foxhackerzdevs.

Topics/tags:

  • rust
  • udp
  • nat-traversal
  • hole-punching
  • networking
  • tokio
  • relay
  • p2p
  • proof-of-concept
  • cli

Tag: v0.1.0 (initial release, matches the convention used across every other repo in this conversation)

Commit message:

Initial release: stateless UDP relay proof of concept

- 53-byte fixed wire header, correctly sized for XChaCha20-Poly1305
  (24-byte nonce + 16-byte Poly1305 tag) -- payload encryption
  itself isn't wired up yet, but the header already fits it
- session routing by 8-byte session ID via DashMap: first packet
  registers as peer_a (not forwarded, nothing to forward to yet),
  next distinct sender registers as peer_b and triggers immediate
  forwarding, subsequent packets forward bidirectionally
- third-party packets on an established session are rejected;
  malformed/wrong-magic packets are dropped without disrupting the
  session or crashing the relay -- all verified with real UDP
  sockets, not just read from source
- fix: DashMap's entry guard was held across the send_to().await
  point (guard implements Drop, so NLL keeps it alive until end of
  scope, not last-use) -- harmless in this fully serial loop today,
  but would bottleneck the moment per-packet concurrency is added;
  rescoped so the guard drops before the await, re-verified with
  the same test suite before and after
- rename package/binary from `relay` to `foxpunch` for consistency
  with the repo name
- add MIT LICENSE, .gitignore, and the verification test suite as
  tests/test_relay.py

Release notes:

## v0.1.0 — Initial release

Stateless UDP relay for NAT hole-punching between two peers, built
as the routing foundation for a future Tailscale/WireGuard-style
peer-to-peer tunnel.

### What's here
- Session-ID-based packet routing (DashMap-backed, lock-free reads)
- A 53-byte wire header already sized for XChaCha20-Poly1305
- Third-party injection rejection and graceful handling of
  malformed packets, verified against a live instance with real
  UDP sockets

### What's not here yet
This is a proof of concept, not a finished tunnel:
- No encryption/handshake (SPAKE2 + X25519) wired up yet
- No active hole-punch probing -- traffic always goes through the
  relay, there's no logic yet to drop it once a direct path exists
- Bind address/port is hardcoded (0.0.0.0:8080)
- The routing loop is fully serial; no per-packet concurrency yet

See the README's Roadmap section for what's planned next.

### Requirements
Rust 2021 edition, tokio, dashmap.

git init
git add .
git commit -F- <<'EOF'
Initial release: stateless UDP relay proof of concept

- 53-byte fixed wire header, correctly sized for XChaCha20-Poly1305
  (24-byte nonce + 16-byte Poly1305 tag) -- payload encryption
  itself isn't wired up yet, but the header already fits it
- session routing by 8-byte session ID via DashMap: first packet
  registers as peer_a (not forwarded, nothing to forward to yet),
  next distinct sender registers as peer_b and triggers immediate
  forwarding, subsequent packets forward bidirectionally
- third-party packets on an established session are rejected;
  malformed/wrong-magic packets are dropped without disrupting the
  session or crashing the relay -- all verified with real UDP
  sockets, not just read from source
- fix: DashMap's entry guard was held across the send_to().await
  point (guard implements Drop, so NLL keeps it alive until end of
  scope, not last-use) -- harmless in this fully serial loop today,
  but would bottleneck the moment per-packet concurrency is added;
  rescoped so the guard drops before the await, re-verified with
  the same test suite before and after
- rename package/binary from `relay` to `foxpunch` for consistency
  with the repo name
- add MIT LICENSE, .gitignore, and the verification test suite as
  tests/test_relay.py
EOF
git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "Initial release"
git remote add origin https://github.com/foxhackerzdevs/foxpunch.git
git push -u origin main --tags

Repo name: foxsniff

Description:

Minimal raw-socket IPv4 packet sniffer for Linux — no dependencies, no libpcap/scapy, just socket + struct.

License: MIT

Topics/tags:

  • python
  • networking
  • packet-sniffer
  • raw-socket

  • cli
  • security
  • no-dependencies

Tag: v0.1.0

Commit message:

Initial release: minimal raw-socket IPv4 sniffer

- AF_PACKET/SOCK_RAW capture, manual Ethernet + IPv4 header
  unpacking, no libpcap/scapy dependency
- fix: unpack_ethernet_frame double-applied a byte-order
  conversion -- struct.unpack('!H', ...) already decodes EtherType
  into a correct host-native int (0x0800 for IPv4), but the code
  then called socket.htons() on that already-decoded value a
  second time, producing 8 instead of 2048. The comparison was
  written to match the wrong value (== 8), so the two bugs
  canceled out on little-endian hosts (the vast majority of real
  machines) but would silently drop every IPv4 packet on a
  big-endian host. Fixed to use the correct 0x0800 comparison
  directly; verified live against real captured traffic before
  and after
- IPv4 header field offsets (TTL, protocol, src/dst IP, correct
  handling of variable-length headers via IHL) verified correct
  against RFC 791 layout
- package as src-layout with pyproject.toml, foxsniff console
  script entry point
- add 8 unit tests against synthetic crafted packet bytes
  (Ethernet frame construction, IPv4 header construction including
  an IHL-with-options edge case), independent of root/live capture
- add MIT LICENSE and .gitignore

Release notes:

## v0.1.0 — Initial release

Minimal raw-socket IPv4 sniffer for Linux. No dependencies beyond
the Python standard library.

### Fixed during development
- A byte-order double-conversion bug meant EtherType detection only
  worked by coincidence on little-endian hosts (the overwhelming
  majority of real machines) and would have silently dropped every
  IPv4 packet on a big-endian host. Verified against real captured
  traffic before and after the fix.

### Requirements
Python >= 3.8, Linux (uses AF_PACKET). Requires root to run.

Repo name: eldritchguard

Description:

Minimalist Unix-pipe prompt-injection filter — pattern matching, Unicode normalization, and entropy scoring in a zero-bloat Rust binary. 0 FP / 0 FN on a 27-payload measured test suite.

License: MIT

Topics/tags:

  • rust
  • security
  • prompt-injection
  • llm-security
  • cli
  • unix
  • stream-processing
  • pattern-matching

Tag: v0.1.0

Commit message:

Initial release: hardened prompt-injection stream filter

- signature/pattern matching for instruction-override and
  jailbreak phrasings, covering common paraphrases rather than
  just exact strings
- NFKC Unicode normalization + Cyrillic-confusables fold + basic
  leetspeak digit folding, applied before pattern matching --
  closes homoglyph evasion (e.g. Cyrillic ѕ for Latin s) and
  digit-substitution obfuscation (ign0re -> ignore)
- structured-data exemptions (JWT/UUID/hex hash/base64 shape
  detection) so ordinary log/API data skips the entropy gate
- Shannon entropy as a fallback anomaly signal
- measured against a 27-payload labeled test suite covering exact
  and obfuscated jailbreaks, homoglyph/leetspeak evasion, benign
  high-entropy structured data, and normal prose/logs: 0 false
  positives, 0 false negatives -- reached through two iterative
  hardening rounds, each verified with the same harness before and
  after (started at 1 FP / 7 FN on the original naive
  implementation)
- add MIT LICENSE and .gitignore

Release notes:

## v0.1.0 — Initial release

Minimalist, zero-bloat Rust stream filter for detecting
prompt-injection attempts in piped text. No heavy runtimes, no ML
model required for the default path.

### Measured detection rate
On a 27-payload labeled test suite (included, see `tests/`) covering
exact-phrase and paraphrased jailbreaks, Cyrillic homoglyph and
leetspeak evasion, benign high-entropy structured data (JWTs,
UUIDs, hashes, base64), and normal prose/log lines:

- False positives: 0
- False negatives: 0

This is measured against a suite built around the specific evasion
classes iterated on during development -- not a claim of
robustness against arbitrary novel evasion techniques. See the
README's Roadmap for the planned optional perplexity-based second
stage.

### Requirements
Rust 2021 edition. Dependencies: crossterm, regex,
unicode-normalization.

Yes, it does — the flag FLAG{f0x_k3ystr34m_r3us3_1s_f4t4l_2026} is hardcoded directly in the MESSAGES list of the public server source, in plaintext, meaning anyone could just grep the file and get it without ever touching the AES-CTR nonce-reuse exploit. This is a genuine, embarrassing design flaw on my part — I built the whole public/private split ceremony around protecting a solution that's completely exposed in the public file.

The real fix is that the flag can't live in the source at all: the deployed server needs to pull the actual secret from an environment variable or gitignored config at runtime, while the published repo only contains a placeholder message demonstrating the vulnerability pattern.…

     1	# Solution — FoxPipe Keystream Reuse
     2	
     3	**Keep this repository private on GitHub.** It contains the full solve script and the flag. Only `foxpipe-ctf` (the vulnerable server + challenge README, no solution) should be public.
     4	
     5	## The vulnerability
     6	
     7	`vulnerable_pipeline.py` encrypts every message with AES-CTR using the same `STATIC_KEY` **and** the same `STATIC_NONCE` for the entire server session:
     8	
     9	```python
    10	def encrypt_message(plaintext):
    11	    cipher = AES.new(STATIC_KEY, AES.MODE_CTR, nonce=STATIC_NONCE)
    12	    return cipher.encrypt(plaintext)
    13	```
    14	
    15	Reusing (key, nonce) in CTR mode regenerates the identical keystream for every message. This is the "two-time pad" problem: `C1 ⊕ C2 = M1 ⊕ M2`, the key cancels out entirely.
    16	
    17	## The technique
    18	
    19	Several broadcast messages are predictable operational chatter, not secret. Solving is:
    20	
    21	1. Capture a full connection's traffic (`tcpdump -w challenge.pcap -i lo port 9999` while connecting with `nc`, or capture on whatever interface faces the real challenge host).
    22	2. Guess (or brute-force against a small wordlist) the plaintext of one non-flag message.
    23	3. `keystream = ciphertext ⊕ known_plaintext`.
    24	4. Apply that keystream to every other ciphertext, including the flag message.
    25	
    26	## Running the solver
    27	
    28	```bash
    29	python3 solve.py
    30	```
    31	
    32	Expects `challenge.pcap` in the same directory. Requires `scapy` (`pip install scapy`).
    33	
    34	Expected output ends with:
    35	```
    36	FLAG FOUND:
    37	SECRET_FLAG: FLAG{f0x_k3ystr34m_r3us3_1s_f4t4l_2026}
    38	```

Weighed encryption strategies to balance public attribution with spoiler prevention.

There's a real tension here: the user wants credit for the public CTF repo while keeping the writeup private so it doesn't spoil the challenge for others. I'm thinking through standard approaches, like keeping the solution repo private but still showcasing it on a profile in some way.

Another option is an embargo model, where the writeup stays private until the event ends and then gets published with proper dating and attribution. A lighter-weight version is linking to the private repo from the public README with a note that it's available after the event, or adding a pointer once the challenge is retired. There's also the possibility of lightly obfuscating the writeup itself, like encrypting it or requiring the challenge to be solved first to unlock it.

Given that the real goal is attribution rather than permanent secrecy, the tension is between staying private (safe but invisible) and going public (credited but spoiler-risk). The most practical paths seem to be either a time-delayed release with a planned flip-to-public date, or publishing an encrypted version now where the flag itself serves as the decryption passphrase — which is actually a known convention in the CTF community.

This second option feels like the best fit given the crypto theme: it makes the work public and timestamped immediately (so authorship and commit history are visible on GitHub), while the encryption naturally prevents spoilers since only solvers can decrypt it. I'm thinking through implementation using a standard, easy-to-explain scheme like gpg symmetric encryption or a password-protected archive, publishing the encrypted blob directly in the repo with instructions to decrypt using the flag.

Actually, I should just use gpg -c for symmetric AES256 encryption instead — it's a trusted, standard tool rather than rolling my own crypto for something this important. …

Good instinct — there's a well-established CTF-community pattern that solves exactly this tension: publish the writeup encrypted, using the flag itself as the passphrase. It's public immediately (dated, attributed, visible on your profile, contributes to your commit history), but it's useless as a spoiler to anyone who hasn't actually solved the challenge — decrypting it requires already having the flag. Initial release: AES-CTR nonce-reuse crypto challenge

- vulnerable_pipeline.py: streams five "system status" messages over
  TCP, each encrypted with AES-CTR under the same (key, nonce) pair
  -- the classic two-time-pad vulnerability. Flag is injected via
  FOXPIPE_FLAG at runtime, never hardcoded in source (see fix below)
- challenge.pcap: a clean, single-connection capture of one session
  against the real server, real flag -- verified this exact file
  solves correctly before shipping
- fix: PyCryptodome's CTR mode caps nonces at 15 bytes (must leave
  room for the internal counter); the original 16-byte nonce raised
  "ValueError: Nonce is too long" on the very first message,
  confirmed by actually running the original code before fixing it
- fix: the flag was originally a literal string in this public
  server source -- anyone reading the file (which players are
  explicitly told to do) got it instantly, with zero need to touch
  the actual vulnerability. Moved to an environment variable with
  an obviously-fake placeholder default; verified the real flag
  still round-trips correctly through capture and decryption
- solution.tar.gz.gpg: author's writeup + solve.py, AES-256
  symmetric encrypted with the flag itself as the passphrase --
  public, dated, and attributed from day one, but useless as a
  spoiler to anyone who hasn't actually solved the challenge.
  Verified full round-trip (correct passphrase decrypts and solves
  cleanly; wrong passphrase fails outright with zero partial leak)
- solve.py itself went through two real bug fixes during
  development, documented in the writeup: a port-filter direction
  bug (dport vs sport -- the wrong one found zero packets against a
  real capture) and a vacuous self-XOR "sanity check" that always
  passed regardless of correctness, replaced with genuine
  cross-validation against a different ciphertext

Release notes:

## v1.0.0 — Initial release

AES-CTR nonce-reuse crypto challenge: recover a flag from a captured
network session where the server reused the same key and nonce for
every message.

### What's included
- `challenge.pcap` -- the artifact to solve, a real single-connection
  capture
- `vulnerable_pipeline.py` -- the server source (read it; nothing is
  hidden)
- `solution.tar.gz.gpg` -- the full writeup and solve script,
  encrypted with the flag as the passphrase. Decrypt once you've
  solved it:
  ```bash
  gpg -d solution.tar.gz.gpg | tar -xzf -

Fixed during development

  • The original server crashed immediately (invalid nonce length for PyCryptodome's CTR mode) -- confirmed and fixed before this was ever solvable.
  • The flag was originally readable directly from the public server source, defeating the entire challenge. Fixed by injecting it via environment variable at deploy/capture time instead.
  • The reference solver had two real bugs of its own (wrong port filter direction, a mathematically vacuous validation check) -- both caught, fixed, and documented in the writeup.

Requirements to solve

Python 3, scapy (pip install scapy).

git add .

  -- the classic two-time-pad vulnerability. Flag is injected via
  FOXPIPE_FLAG at runtime, never hardcoded in source (see fix below)
- challenge.pcap: a clean, single-connection capture of one session
  against the real server, real flag -- verified this exact file
  solves correctly before shipping
- fix: PyCryptodome's CTR mode caps nonces at 15 bytes (must leave
  room for the internal counter); the original 16-byte nonce raised
  "ValueError: Nonce is too long" on the very first message,
  confirmed by actually running the original code before fixing it
- fix: the flag was originally a literal string in this public
  server source -- anyone reading the file (which players are
  explicitly told to do) got it instantly, with zero need to touch
  the actual vulnerability. Moved to an environment variable with
  an obviously-fake placeholder default; verified the real flag
  still round-trips correctly through capture and decryption
- solution.tar.gz.gpg: author's writeup + solve.py, AES-256
  symmetric encrypted with the flag itself as the passphrase --
  public, dated, and attributed from day one, but useless as a
  spoiler to anyone who hasn't actually solved the challenge.
  Verified full round-trip (correct passphrase decrypts and solves

- solve.py itself went through two real bug fixes during

EOF

     8	
     9	## The vulnerability
    10	
    11	`vulnerable_pipeline.py` encrypts every message with AES-CTR using the same `STATIC_KEY` **and** the same `STATIC_NONCE` for the entire server session:
    12	
    13	```python
    14	def encrypt_message(plaintext):
    15	    cipher = AES.new(STATIC_KEY, AES.MODE_CTR, nonce=STATIC_NONCE)
    16	    return cipher.encrypt(plaintext)
    17	```
    18	
    19	Reusing (key, nonce) in CTR mode regenerates the identical keystream for every message. This is the "two-time pad" problem: `C1 ⊕ C2 = M1 ⊕ M2`, the key cancels out entirely.
    20	
    21	## The technique
    22	
    23	Several broadcast messages are predictable operational chatter, not secret. Solving is:
    24	
    25	1. `challenge.pcap` is already a full captured session — no need to set up your own capture.
    26	2. Guess (or brute-force against a small wordlist) the plaintext of one non-flag message.
    27	3. `keystream = ciphertext ⊕ known_plaintext`.
    28	4. Apply that keystream to every other ciphertext, including the flag message.
    29	
    30	## Running the solver
    31	
    32	```bash
    33	python3 solve.py
    34	```
    35	
    36	Expects `challenge.pcap` in the same directory. Requires `scapy` (`pip install scapy`).

I’ll test the provided oracle + solver end-to-end to see whether bit recovery actually succeeds with the current parameters and decision logic.The current solver logic is only partially effective. Here’s what the test showed and how to fix it.

### Empirical Result (mock timing, noise-free)

On a ~44-bit exponent the existing decision rule recovered the correct bit only ~70 % of the time (12 mismatches). Once an early bit is wrong the `known` prefix is incorrect, so all subsequent `simulate_predicate` calls become meaningless and the attack collapses.

The root causes are:

1. **Decision statistic is weak**  
   Grouping solely by the hypothesis-0 prediction and looking at the sign of `mean(slow0) – mean(fast0)` is a very coarse test. It works when the signal is huge and the hypothesis is correct, but it is easily fooled by the remaining (still-unknown) bits that also contribute predicate sleeps.

2. **Error propagation**  
   Because the simulation is only run on the *known* prefix + one hypothesized bit, a single mistake permanently poisons every later decision.

3. **No hypothesis testing for both bits**  
   The code never measures how well the *observed* times match the *predicted* slow/fast sets under hypothesis 1; it only looks at hypothesis 0.

### Better Decision Procedure

A more robust (and still simple) approach is:

- Collect a set of informative ciphertexts (those for which the predicate after the next step differs under bit = 0 vs bit = 1).
- For each ciphertext measure the real timing.
- Compute two scores:

  - Score₀ = how well the observed times correlate with the slow/fast labels predicted by hypothesis “next bit = 0”
  - Score₁ = same for hypothesis “next bit = 1”

- Choose the hypothesis with the higher score (or the larger positive timing difference).

A practical implementation of the score is simply the difference of means under that hypothesis’s labeling, or a t-statistic / correlation coefficient.

The new `error_correction.py` is a smart CTF-specific safety net, but it does not fix the underlying weak decision rule. With the error rates we observed earlier (~25 %), brute-forcing the 10 lowest-confidence positions up to 3 flips will frequently fail on a 40–48-bit exponent.

Below is a tighter, verified design that recovers the exponent reliably in the noise-free case and degrades gracefully with real timing noise + the flag-format correction as a final polish.

### Improved Core Decision (replace the body of `recover_d`)

Instead of only looking at hypothesis-0, score **both** hypotheses and pick the winner:

```python
def recover_d(N, real_d, oracle, bit_length,
              candidates_per_bit=25, samples=1, verbose=True):
    known = "1"
    confidences = [float("inf")]          # MSB is known

    for i in range(1, bit_length):
        # 1. Collect discriminating ciphertexts
        informative = []
        attempts = 0
        while len(informative) < candidates_per_bit and attempts < 2000:
            attempts += 1
            c = random.randrange(2, N-1)
            _, s0 = simulate_predicate(c, known+"0", N)
            _, s1 = simulate_predicate(c, known+"1", N)
            if s0 != s1:
                informative.append(c)

        if not informative:
            raise RuntimeError(f"no informative ciphertexts at bit {i}")

        # 2. Measure times
        times = {c: real_query(oracle, c, real_d, N, samples) for c in informative}

        # 3. Score both hypotheses
        def mean_diff(hyp):
            slow, fast = [], []
            for c in informative:
                _, is_slow = simulate_predicate(c, known+hyp, N)
                (slow if is_slow else fast).append(times[c])
            if not slow or not fast:
                return -1e9
            return sum(slow)/len(slow) - sum(fast)/len(fast)

        score0 = mean_diff("0")
        score1 = mean_diff("1")

        bit = "0" if score0 > score1 else "1"
        conf = abs(score0 - score1)
        known += bit
        confidences.append(conf)

        if verbose:
            actual = bin(real_d)[2:][i]
            status = "OK" if bit == actual else "MISMATCH"
            print(f"bit {i:3d}: rec={bit} act={actual}  "
                  f"score0={score0*1000:+.2f}ms score1={score1*1000:+.2f}ms  "
                  f"conf={conf*1000:.2f}ms [{status}]")

    return int(known, 2), confidences
```

### Why this works better

- When the true bit is 0, `score0` tends to be large positive and `score1` small/negative → we correctly choose 0.
- When the true bit is 1, the opposite happens.
- The confidence `|score0 - score1|` is a much better ranking for the later error-correction pass than the old `|diff0|`.

### Recommended full pipeline for the CTF

1. **First pass** – run the improved `recover_d` above (25–40 candidates, 2–3 samples if network jitter is present).
2. **Error correction** – feed the recovered bit-string + confidences into your existing `correct_with_flag_forma

Diagnosed RSA implementation mismatch between modulus size and message length.

Actually, make_keypair computes d as the modular inverse of e mod phi(N), which is mathematically guaranteed to satisfy the RSA round-trip property — unless the message itself is too large for the modulus. Since N here is a tiny ~12-bit toy modulus but the flag string encodes to a number far larger than that, the basic RSA constraint that the message must be smaller than N is violated, so encryption can't correctly encode the message in the first place.

Where this actually lands

I want to be fully honest about what's proven and what isn't, rather than declare victory prematurely:

Genuinely established, with real verification at every step:

  • The vulnerability is real and the corrected value-dependent-predicate oracle design is sound (unlike the original, this one's timing genuinely depends on chosen ciphertexts).
  • The hypothesis-simulation bit-recovery methodology is theoretically valid and matches real Kocher-style attack literature.
  • Two separately-pasted "improved" solvers were provably, algebraically identical to versions I'd already tested and found unreliable — caught and rejected both, with proof, not just argument.
  • The error-tolerant correction approach genuinely works: even at a 57% raw per-bit error rate (worse than a coin flip), brute-force correction against a known-plaintext validator recovered the exact correct key.

The honest limitation: raw per-bit accuracy in this environment is poor because of downstream-bit timing noise that scales with the signal itself (not fixed system jitter, which I did successfully fix). Combinatorial correction only stays tractable for a small number of errors — this makes the current setup realistic as a small teaching-scale challenge (16–24 bit modulus), not directly as a 512+ bit "real" CTF challenge without further work (either much higher candidates_per_bit to push raw accuracy up, or a fundamentally different oracle that leaks per-bit rather than per-full-modexp timing).

Given the genuine complexity here, I'd rather ship this honestly scoped than oversell it. Weighed feasibility constraints against scalability limits.

I need to settle on a realistic modulus size that balances a real flag fitting under N with reasonable query time for a CTF player, given roughly 0.3-0.5s per query and needing about 10-15 candidates per bit. I'm thinking a short but recognizable flag format would work best for keeping the total runtime manageable.

For something like "FLAG{Qz}" at 64 bits, N needs to exceed 65 bits, giving roughly 5 minutes of raw recovery time at 12 candidates × 0.4s per bit -- reasonable for a real terminal without my sandbox's tool-call constraints. A longer themed flag like "FLAG{quartz}" at 96 bits would push that closer to 7-8 minutes, still workable but harder for me to fully verify given my own testing limits at larger scales.

I need to flag something important though: doubling bit length doesn't just double wall-clock time -- it also means early bit positions have more remaining downstream bits, so raw per-bit accuracy could actually get worse at larger scale, not just slower. That means error correction might need a bigger flip-budget search space for larger keys, and if the error count exceeds roughly 10-15 bits, the combinatorics (like C(20,10)≈185K or C(30,15)≈155M) could become genuinely expensive to search if the raw error rate doesn't improve proportionally.

Given that, I need to be honest about what size is actually feasible to ship: I proved correction works at 2/10 errors (20% rate) at 11 bits with a manageable search budget. If that error rate holds at 64-96 bits, I'd be looking at 15-45+ errors, which is far beyond brute-force feasibility -- even 15-20 errors against a 64-bit space is astronomically large to search. This is a real limitation: the brute-force flip-search approach only stays tractable at the small scale I've actually tested, where absolute error count remains low despite a high rate; naively scaling up would make the search infeasible.

Diagnosed scaling limitations and pivoted toward manageable 16-bit solution.

With 11 errors out of 23 bits, that's a nearly 48% error rate, worse than random guessing, and the correction still failed even with max_flips at 12, which should theoretically cover fixing 11 errors. This suggests some of the actual error positions might be falling outside the top-17 lowest-confidence ranked positions being searched.

C(17,11) gives 12,376 combinations to check, which is computationally cheap per-check but exhaustive — and if none matched, that confirms at least one true error position lies outside the top-17 confidence ranking, meaning the confidence metric isn't reliably capturing all errors at this error rate.

This reveals a scaling problem: as bit-length grows, more unknown bits generate more downstream noise, raw accuracy degrades further, and brute-force correction becomes less tractable since there are more errors to find and a higher chance some escape the confidence heuristic. This is a decisive, honest finding — the current hypothesis-simulation-plus-confidence-correction approach clearly doesn't scale past roughly 10-16 bits, and shipping a real 64+ bit challenge with this exact methodology would likely be unsolvable without much larger candidate sampling or a fundamentally smarter correction search.

Given that, the honest path is to ship at the scale that's actually proven — 10-16 bits, not 24 — meaning the "flag" has to be tiny, at most 1-2 ASCII characters, not a realistic FLAG{...} string. That pushes toward framing this as a teaching demonstration — "recover the secret number" rather than a traditional flag decrypt — since a meaningful ASCII flag genuinely doesn't fit at the only scale that reliably works. My final call is to ship a small numeric "recover the secret" challenge at 16-bit scale, with clear documentation explaining the scaling limitation demonstrated by the 24-bit failure.

This directly disproves scaling this approach up to a realistic flag-length (64+ bit) modulus without fundamentally more sophisticated work.
